questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL transaction allocates an invoice ID with `nextval` and then rolls back. What happens to that allocation?

choices.text: The value is reused after rollback.
The sequence value stays consumed.
The rollback rewinds every session to the previous sequence value.
The sequence keeps the value only if the failed insert reached commit.

questions.explanation: Sequence allocation is not rolled back, so gaps are expected. Atomic allocation prevents concurrent sessions from receiving the same nextval result.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.17. Sequence Manipulation Functions
sources.claim: nextval is atomic and is not rolled back; currval is session-local and requires a previous nextval in that session.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL transaction issues `NOTIFY jobs` and stays open. When may listening sessions receive that notification?

choices.text: Immediately, before the sender commits.
After the next checkpoint, even if the sender rolls back its changes.
After the sender commits.
Only after all listening sessions disconnect and reconnect again.

questions.explanation: NOTIFY participates in transaction commit. An aborted transaction sends nothing; checkpoints and listener reconnections do not control delivery.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: NOTIFY
sources.claim: NOTIFY is delivered only after commit; notifications with the same channel and payload within one transaction may be folded into one.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL service coordinates work with advisory locks. Which properties should its design account for? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Session-level advisory locks survive a transaction rollback.
Transaction-level advisory locks release when the transaction ends.
Application code must cooperate on the same lock keys.
Ordinary table writes are blocked whenever any advisory key is locked.
Rolling back a transaction releases every session-level advisory lock it acquired.

questions.explanation: A is correct: session locks follow session lifetime rather than transaction rollback. B is correct: commit or rollback releases transaction locks. C is correct: advisory locks do not automatically enforce business rules. D is incorrect: advisory locks are separate from automatic table and row locks. E is incorrect: session locks require explicit release or session termination.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 13.3. Explicit Locking
sources.claim: Session advisory locks survive transaction rollback; transaction advisory locks release at transaction end; advisory locks are cooperative.

questions.prompt: A fresh PostgreSQL session calls `currval` for a sequence it has never advanced. What should its caller expect?

choices.text: The latest value from any session.
The sequence start value even if another session has advanced it.
The most recent committed row ID from a table using that sequence.
An error in that session.

questions.explanation: currval reports the value last obtained by nextval in the current session. It is undefined before that session has called nextval, regardless of other sessions.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.17. Sequence Manipulation Functions
sources.claim: nextval is atomic and is not rolled back; currval is session-local and requires a previous nextval in that session.

questions.prompt: One PostgreSQL transaction sends the same channel and payload three times with NOTIFY. Which delivery behavior is documented?

choices.text: Duplicate notifications can be folded.
Three deliveries are always required.
All notifications on that channel are discarded until another payload appears.
The payload is concatenated three times into one notification automatically.

questions.explanation: Identical channel/payload notifications in one transaction can be combined. Different payloads remain distinct, and folding does not concatenate their contents.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: NOTIFY
sources.claim: NOTIFY is delivered only after commit; notifications with the same channel and payload within one transaction may be folded into one.

questions.prompt: A connection pool uses PostgreSQL session advisory locks for tenant jobs. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A transaction advisory lock needs a matching manual unlock after commit.
An unrelated SQL client must acquire the advisory key before updating rows.
A session advisory lock becomes transaction-scoped whenever BEGIN is used.
Explicit unlock calls matter before a pooled connection is reused.
Repeated acquisition of one session lock requires matching unlocks.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: transaction locks release automatically at transaction end. B is incorrect: advisory locking is voluntary and does not impose that SQL prerequisite. C is incorrect: BEGIN does not change the lifetime of a session-level lock. D is correct: session locks can outlive one borrower transaction. E is correct: session advisory lock requests stack.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 13.3. Explicit Locking
sources.claim: Session advisory locks survive transaction rollback; transaction advisory locks release at transaction end; advisory locks are cooperative.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, session A begins a transaction, calls `pg_advisory_lock(42)` twice, calls `pg_advisory_unlock(42)` once, then rolls back. A stays connected. Session B now requests the same exclusive key. What happens?

choices.text: B obtains the key because rollback released A's session locks.
B waits because A still has one unreleased acquisition.
B obtains the key because one unlock clears all nested acquisitions.
B raises an error because session locks cannot be acquired inside BEGIN.

questions.explanation: Session locks can be acquired inside transactions but do not obey transaction rollback. Two acquisitions need two unlocks. One hold remains, so B waits for A to unlock again or end its session. Neither rollback nor a single unlock releases every acquisition.

sources.title: Explicit locking: advisory locks
sources.claim: Session advisory locks survive rollback and require matching unlocks; transaction locks release at transaction end; both scopes conflict on the same key and require cooperation.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, A holds an exclusive transaction advisory lock for key 42. B, a different session, requests a session advisory lock for key 42. A then commits. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: B waits while A holds the same exclusive key.
A must explicitly unlock the transaction lock after committing.
Committing releases A's transaction advisory lock.
The advisory lock automatically rejects every ordinary table write.
Code that never requests advisory keys is not coordinated by this lock.

questions.explanation: A: transaction and session locks conflict on the same exclusive key. C: transaction locks release automatically at transaction end, so B can proceed. E: advisory locking is cooperative. B is false because no manual transaction unlock is required; D is false because ordinary writes do not automatically participate.

sources.title: Explicit locking: advisory locks
sources.claim: Session advisory locks survive rollback and require matching unlocks; transaction locks release at transaction end; both scopes conflict on the same key and require cooperation.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL sequence uses increment 1 and CACHE 1. With no other callers or resets, A executes `setval(s, 100, false)` inside a transaction and then rolls back. B next calls `nextval(s)`. Which value does B get?

choices.text: The value from before A called setval.
An error until A commits the setval transaction.

questions.explanation: setval changes are not undone by rollback. Its false is_called argument makes the next nextval return exactly 100 rather than advance to 101. Rollback neither restores the earlier state nor requires A to commit before B can use the sequence.

sources.title: Sequence manipulation functions
sources.claim: setval changes are visible to other transactions and not undone by rollback; with is_called false the next nextval returns exactly the specified value.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, A gets 10 from `nextval(s)`, then B gets 11 from the same sequence. Neither session resets it. Later an INSERT evaluates `nextval(s)` but uses `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Which conclusions are valid? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A's `currval(s)` now returns B's value 11.
A's `currval(s)` remains 10 until A advances or sets that sequence.
The conflicting INSERT can consume a sequence value without inserting a row.
Every gap between row IDs proves that a committed row was deleted.
Sequences do not guarantee gapless committed row IDs.

questions.explanation: B: currval is local to the session, so B does not change A's result. C: the tuple and its nextval are evaluated before the conflict is detected. E: aborted or conflicting inserts can leave gaps. A confuses session-local state with the global sequence, and D ignores allocations that never produced committed rows.

sources.title: Sequence manipulation functions
sources.claim: nextval allocations are not reclaimed on abort or ON CONFLICT; currval is session-local; sequences are not gapless.
